::: callout-note
## Biological question

A camera trap takes thousands of photos, a microscope thousands of cells, a recorder
hours of bird songs. Nobody can look at all of them. What can a machine learn to see for
us, how does it learn it, and when should we trust it?
:::

Everybody talks about artificial intelligence (AI). Today you open the box. You start by
**annotating photos** yourself, as thousands of volunteers do for research projects; then
you write rules by hand to recognise penguin species, and let a computer **learn** the same
rules from examples. You build a **random forest** with your own hands, train a small
**neural network**, and compute by hand what the first layer of a **deep** network does
to a camera-trap photo. Finally you read the results of a real deep-learning model trained
on amphibians crossing a railway. Then you open the most famous AI of biology,
**AlphaFold**: you download the predicted structure of *FLC* (the flowering gene of
Session 6), read it as a table, judge how much to trust it, and understand how an alignment
of related sequences tells AlphaFold which amino acids touch. Finally you explore the AI
tools biologists use every day.

Since Session 4 you have used models to **explain** (does drought change diversity? which
SNP is associated with flowering?). Today the goal changes: models that **predict**, and
the one question that matters for them: how good are they on data they have never seen?

::: callout-important
## How you work today: nothing is graded

**Today nothing is graded and there is nothing to submit.** Take your time, try things,
ask questions: the goal is that you understand what artificial intelligence does, because
you will meet it, use it and judge it during your whole career.

First comes the whole lecture, in four parts, then the practical. The practical follows the
lecture in the same order: when you start a block, scroll back to its theory part (each
block says which one). **The code is short on purpose**: a tree is one line, a neural network one line. As in Session 6, you work
in `WORKBOOK.qmd`; **Render** makes `WORKBOOK.pdf`, your own notes of the day, to keep.
The day ends with block G, on **AlphaFold**, the most famous AI of biology: start it in
class, and finish it after. Every chunk runs in a few seconds.
:::

### Learning outcomes

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

- explain the difference between a program written with rules and a model that learns
  from examples, and place AI, machine learning and deep learning in each other;
- use the vocabulary: label, feature, training, validation and test sets, model,
  prediction, parameter (weight), loss, epoch, overfitting;
- train and read a decision tree, and explain why a random forest of trees votes better;
- read a confusion matrix, and compute an accuracy, a recall and a precision;
- explain what a neuron, a layer, a convolution and a filter are, and why deep learning
  works on photos where rules fail;
- say where the labels of a model come from, and why an accuracy can hide a model that is
  poor on rare species;
- explain how AlphaFold predicts a structure from a sequence (alignment, coevolution,
  training on known structures), download a prediction and judge it with its pLDDT and
  PAE;
- choose an AI tool for a biological question, and check its answer.

## Before the lecture: annotate

Before any explanation: open the link given by the instructor on your phone or laptop and
annotate as many photos as you can, carefully. Answers given too fast do not count.

## Theory 1: what is artificial intelligence? {#theory-1}

### Chihuahua or muffin?

In 2016, the artist Karen Zack posted grids of photos where chihuahuas and blueberry
muffins look almost the same: two dark eyes and a nose, or three blueberries. You see the
difference in a fraction of a second. Now try to **write the rule**: "if there are three
dark round spots in a triangle, then...". It does not work: the dog can turn its head, the
muffin can have four blueberries, the light changes. Computer-vision services were tested
on these grids ([Chihuahua or muffin? My search for the best computer vision
API](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/chihuahua-or-muffin-my-search-for-the-best-computer-vision-api-cbda4d6b425d/),
2017): they mostly succeed, and nobody wrote their rules.

This is the whole idea of machine learning: **when we cannot write the rules, we give the
computer examples with the right answer, and it finds the rules itself.**

### AI, machine learning, deep learning

| Term | What it means | Example in biology |
|---|---|---|
| **Artificial intelligence** (AI) | Any program that does a task we would call intelligent if a person did it. Includes rules written by people. | An identification key coded as a program. |
| **Machine learning** (ML) | AI that **learns its rules from examples** instead of being programmed with them. | A decision tree that predicts the species from 4 measures (today, block B). |
| **Deep learning** (DL) | Machine learning with **neural networks of many layers**, which also learn *what to look at* (the features) from raw data: pixels, sounds, sequences. | A network that finds toads in camera-trap photos (block F); AlphaFold. |

Each is inside the previous one: all deep learning is machine learning, all machine
learning is AI, not the other way round. **Generative AI** (chatbots such as ChatGPT,
Claude, Le Chat; image generators) is deep learning trained to *produce* text or images
rather than to classify them.

### The families of learning

- **Supervised learning**: examples come with the answer (the **label**): photo → "toad".
  The model learns to predict the label. *Today.*
- **Unsupervised learning**: no label; the model finds structure by itself. *The PCA and
  the clustering of Session 5.*
- **Self-supervised learning**: the model makes its own labels from the data (hide a word
  and guess it, hide a piece of a protein sequence and guess it). How chatbots and protein
  language models are trained.

And the main **tasks**, all present in the AnnoTrain projects of the instructor:

| Task | Question | Output | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classification | Which class? | One label per photo | Animal or not; which amphibian species |
| Regression | How much? | A number | Age of a fish from a scale; leaf area |
| Detection | Where are the objects? | A box around each | Each animal in a camera-trap photo |
| Segmentation | Which pixels belong to what? | A mask | Roots, shoots and seeds on a plate; each cell of a tissue |
| Tracking | Where does each object go? | A path per individual | Fish swimming in a video |
| Generation | Produce something new | Text, image, sequence | A chatbot's answer; a designed protein |

### The vocabulary of supervised learning

- A **dataset** is a table (or a set of photos), one row per **observation** (a penguin,
  a photo).
- The **features** are what the model may look at (the measures, the pixels); the
  **label** is what it must predict (the species).
- The **model** is the recipe that turns features into a prediction; its **parameters**
  (for a network: its **weights**) are the numbers it learns. The settings chosen by
  people before training (the size of a tree, the number of neurons) are
  **hyperparameters**.
- **Training** adjusts the parameters so that the predictions match the labels of the
  **training set**. A **validation set** is used to choose hyperparameters and when to
  stop; a **test set**, never touched before the end, tells how good the model is.
- **Inference** (or prediction) is using the trained model on new data.

The golden rule, which you already met with the cross-validation of Session 5: **a model is
only judged on data it has never seen.**

### Is the model good? The confusion matrix

Rows: the truth. Columns: what the model said. A camera trap, 100 photos, 30 with an
animal:

| | predicted: animal | predicted: empty |
|---|---:|---:|
| **true: animal** | 24 (true positives) | 6 (false negatives: missed) |
| **true: empty** | 4 (false positives: invented) | 66 (true negatives) |

- **Accuracy** = correct / all = (24 + 66) / 100 = 0.90.
- **Recall** of "animal" = found / all true animals = 24 / 30 = 0.80. *Did we miss
  animals?*
- **Precision** of "animal" = right / all called animal = 24 / 28 = 0.86. *When it says
  animal, can we believe it?*
- The **F1 score** combines both: 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall).

**The accuracy trap.** A model that answers "empty" for every photo, without looking, has
an accuracy of 70 / 100 = 0.70 here, and a recall of 0 for animals. In real camera-trap
projects most photos are empty, and most annotated photos belong to a few common species:
always look at the recall of each class, especially the rare ones.

## Theory 2: learning or memorising? {#theory-2}

### A decision tree

A **decision tree** asks yes/no questions on the features, one after the other. For three
trees of a park, from their leaves: "leaf longer than 12 cm?" → chestnut; otherwise
"margin toothed?" → beech if no, hornbeam if yes. To build it, the computer tries every feature and every threshold, and keeps the
question that separates the labels best; then it does the same in each half, and so on.
It is a dichotomous identification key, but **learned from examples**. It is easy to read,
which is its great strength.

### Overfitting

A tree allowed to grow without limit ends with one leaf per training example: it is then
100% right on the training data, by heart. This is **overfitting**: the model learns the
noise and the peculiarities of the training examples instead of a rule that generalises.
The signature: very good on the training set, much worse on the test set. The opposite,
**underfitting**, is a model too simple to capture the rule (a tree with one question for
three species). You will see it with shuffled labels (as in Session 5): the tree reaches
100% on training labels that mean nothing.

### A random forest

One tree is unstable: change a few training examples and it changes. A **random forest**
(Breiman, 2001) grows hundreds of trees, each on a **bootstrap** sample (the training
examples drawn again at random, with replacement) and with a random subset of the
features, then lets them **vote**. Each tree is wrong sometimes, but not on the same
examples: the errors cancel out in the majority. It is the same idea as asking several
people to annotate the same photo. Random forests are still among the best models for
tables of measurements, and the classical pixel classifier of
[ilastik](https://www.ilastik.org) is one.

### A neuron is a linear model

An artificial **neuron** computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a constant, then
passes it through an **activation function**:

$$\text{output} = f(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + w_3 x_3 + b)$$

The part inside $f$ is exactly the `lm()` of Session 4: weights (slopes) and an intercept.
The activation $f$ bends it: **ReLU** keeps positive values and sets negative ones to 0; the
**sigmoid** squeezes the result between 0 and 1, like a probability. A **layer** is many
neurons side by side; a **network** stacks layers, the outputs of one being the inputs of
the next. With enough neurons, a network can draw any boundary between classes.

**Training** a network means finding the weights that make the **loss** (the error between
predictions and labels) as small as possible. The algorithm, **gradient descent**, is a
walker in the fog going down a hill: at each step it measures the slope of the loss for
each weight and moves the weights a little downhill. One pass over all the training
examples is an **epoch**; a network trains for tens of epochs.

## Theory 3: deep learning for images {#theory-3}

### A photo is a table of numbers

A grey photo is a matrix: one number per pixel, from 0 (black) to 255 (white). A colour
photo is three matrices (red, green, blue). A camera-trap photo of 2,048 × 1,494 pixels is
9 million numbers. A tree asking "is pixel 15,200 brighter than 120?" is useless: the
animal can be anywhere, at any size, in any light. What matters are **shapes**, made by
many pixels together.

### Before deep learning: features designed by people

Until about 2012, image analysis started with **features designed by people**: brightness,
colour, edges, textures, computed by hand-written formulas, then given to a classifier
such as a random forest. It works on simple, well-controlled images (the instructor's
2025 lecture on root images shows this with ilastik), and fails on the variety of the
real world.

### Convolution: filters that slide over the photo

A **filter** (or kernel) is a small grid of numbers, for example 3 × 3. It slides over the
photo; at each position, it multiplies the 9 pixels under it by its 9 numbers and adds
them up. This is a **convolution**. With −1 on the left and +1 on the right, the result is
large where the photo changes from dark to light: the filter detects vertical edges. You
will compute it yourself in block E. Then come **ReLU** (keep the positive answers) and
**pooling** (keep the largest value of each 2 × 2 square, which halves the size of the
image and keeps what was found).

A **convolutional neural network** (CNN) is a stack of such layers. The key: **the numbers
of the filters are weights, learned during training.** The first layers learn edges and
colours, the next ones combine them into textures and corners, the deeper ones into parts
(an eye, a leg, a leaf margin) and whole objects. Nobody writes the features any more:
they are learned from annotated examples. See them for yourself in the [Feature
Visualization](https://distill.pub/2017/feature-visualization/) article.

### Why it took off around 2012

Three things came together: **data** (ImageNet, 14 million annotated photos, built by
people annotating online), **computing power** (graphics cards, GPUs, which do millions of
multiplications at once) and better **architectures**. In 2012 a CNN (AlexNet) won the
ImageNet challenge by a large margin; in 2015, **ResNet** (He et al.) went past 150 layers.
The ResNet-18 used by AnnoTrain has 18 layers and about 11 million weights.

### Transfer learning: you do not start from zero

Training 11 million weights needs millions of photos. But the first layers of a network
trained on ImageNet (edges, textures, shapes) are useful for any photo. **Transfer
learning** (or fine-tuning) starts from such a network and retrains it on a few hundred or
thousand annotated photos of your own question. This is how AnnoTrain, Teachable Machine
and most biology tools work.

### Where the labels come from

A supervised model is only as good as its labels. They come from people: experts,
students, volunteers of citizen-science platforms such as
[Zooniverse](https://www.zooniverse.org) or [iNaturalist](https://www.inaturalist.org).
People make mistakes and disagree, so projects ask several people per photo and keep the
**consensus** (the majority). This "**ground truth**" is never perfectly true. Two classic
traps: **class imbalance** (a few common species, many rare ones with almost no examples),
and **domain shift**: a model trained on some cameras or some microscopes is often much
worse on new ones (Beery et al., 2018).

### AnnoTrain

[AnnoTrain](https://annotrain.cmaslard.xyz) is the instructor's open platform that puts the
whole chain in one place: a researcher creates a project and shares a link; people
annotate (open the link, answer, next photo); the platform builds the consensus, checks
the answers (too-fast answers and people who disagree with reference photos do not
count), trains a network (ResNet-18 for classification, detectors, U-Net and Cellpose for
segmentation), and shows its training curves, its confusion matrix and its mistakes. You
can use it for your Master's project: the goal is to annotate fast, together, and to get
a first model without writing code.

::: callout-note
## The whole chain

Raw photos → **annotation** by people → **consensus** (the labels) → **training set /
validation set** → **training** (epochs, loss) → **evaluation** (confusion matrix, recall
per class) → **model** → **prediction** on new photos → people check the uncertain ones →
new labels → a better model.
:::

## Theory 4: AlphaFold, how a structure is predicted {#theory-4}

### The problem: 50 years old

A protein is a chain of amino acids that folds into a precise 3D shape, and the shape makes
the function: a pocket that binds a molecule, a surface that grips DNA, a pore that lets
sodium through. In 1972, Christian Anfinsen received the Nobel Prize for showing that the
sequence alone contains the information of the fold. But reading it was another matter:
solving one structure by experiment (X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, NMR)
takes months to years. The Protein Data Bank ([PDB](https://www.rcsb.org)) holds about
200,000 solved structures, while hundreds of millions of protein sequences are known.
Since 1994, a blind competition, [CASP](https://predictioncenter.org), asks teams to predict
structures that have just been solved but not yet published. In 2020, AlphaFold 2 (Google
DeepMind) predicted most of them with an accuracy close to the experiments. In 2024, Demis
Hassabis and John Jumper shared the [Nobel Prize in
Chemistry](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2024/summary/) for it (with David
Baker, for protein design).

### The idea: amino acids that touch evolve together

AlphaFold starts as you did in Session 3: it **searches databases for related sequences**
(hundreds to thousands, from all living beings) and **aligns them**: a multiple sequence
alignment (MSA). Two kinds of information come out of it:

- **conservation**: a position that never changes is probably important (the core of the
  protein, the active site);
- **coevolution**: if two positions always change *together*, they are probably in
  contact in 3D. A positive lysine (K) facing a negative glutamate (E) holds the fold; if a
  mutation turns the K into an E, the protein unfolds, unless the partner also turns into a
  K. Over millions of years, such pairs leave a signature of correlated changes in the
  alignment. You will find one in a small made-up alignment (block G6).

### From a sequence to a structure, step by step

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart TB
  A["Step 1: Sequence: MGRKKLEIKR... (196 amino acids)"] --> B["Step 2: Search: related sequences (alignment) and known structures"]
  B --> C["Step 3: Evoformer x 48: the alignment table and the pair table talk to each other"]
  C --> D["Step 4: Structure module: the 3D position of every atom"]
  D -- "Step 5: recycling x 3" --> C
  D --> E["Step 6: Output: structure + pLDDT + PAE"]
```

**1. The input** is only the sequence of the protein, the letters you met in the FASTA files
of Session 1.

**2. The search.** AlphaFold searches huge databases for related sequences: UniProt, but
also billions of sequences read directly from environmental DNA (soils, oceans, guts:
metagenomes). It aligns them (a multiple sequence alignment, as with MAFFT in Session 3),
often thousands of rows. It also looks for related proteins whose structure was solved
by experiment (**templates**). This step takes most of the computing time of a
prediction, before any neural network runs.

**3. The Evoformer: two tables that talk to each other.** The network keeps two tables
and improves them 48 times in a row:

- the **alignment table**: one row per related sequence, one column per position of the
  protein;
- the **pair table**: one cell for every pair of positions (196 × 196 for *FLC*), holding
  the network's current belief about how these two amino acids sit relative to each other
  in space. Think of it as the contact map you will draw in G4, but richer.

Each block of the Evoformer uses **attention**: every position looks at all the others and
decides, with learned weights, which ones to listen to, as you would scan a page for the
words that matter. Information flows both ways: two columns of the alignment that change
together write "probably close" into the pair table (coevolution); the pair table in turn
tells the network where to look in the alignment. A special step, the **triangle
update**, checks every trio of amino acids: if A is close to B and B is close to C, then A
cannot be 50 Å from C. The network was never taught geometry: it learned these rules from
the examples.

**4. The structure module.** Each amino acid starts as a small rigid triangle (its
backbone atoms N, Cα and C) floating at the same point. The module moves and turns every
triangle, step by step, until their positions agree with the pair table, then places the
side chains. The result: x, y, z coordinates for every atom, the numbers you will read in
the PDB file in G1.

**5. Recycling.** The whole structure is fed back into the Evoformer, and everything runs
again, three times: each pass corrects the previous one.

**6. The confidence scores.** During training, the network also learned to predict **its
own error**: the pLDDT for each amino acid, the PAE for each pair. That is why AlphaFold
can say "here, I do not know" (next section).

### How it learned

Like everything today, AlphaFold is **supervised learning**. The examples: about 170,000
structures of the Protein Data Bank solved by experiment, each with its sequence. The
label: the experimental 3D structure. The loss: for each amino acid, stand on it, look at
all the other atoms, and measure how far they are from where they should be. Two more
tricks:

- **fill in the blanks**: some letters of the alignment are hidden, and the network must
  guess them, exactly like the `___` of your workbook. To guess a hidden letter, it has to
  understand which positions depend on which: it learns coevolution by itself;
- **learning from its own best guesses**: the first version predicted about 350,000
  proteins of unknown structure; the predictions it was very sure of were added to the
  training examples.

Training took about two weeks on 128 specialised processors (Google TPUs). A prediction
then takes minutes to hours: the weights are learned once, and reused for every protein.

### Two scores to judge a prediction

- The **pLDDT** (0-100), for each amino acid: how sure AlphaFold is of the local structure.
  Above 90 very high, 70-90 confident, 50-70 low, below 50 very low. On the website: dark
  blue, light blue, yellow, orange. A very low pLDDT often means that this part of the
  protein is really **disordered** in the cell (it has no fixed shape), which is itself
  useful information.
- The **PAE** (predicted aligned error), for each pair of amino acids: if the prediction is
  superposed on the true structure using amino acid A, how far off (in Å) will amino acid B
  be? Small inside a domain, large between two domains linked by a flexible piece:
  AlphaFold can be sure of the shape of each domain and unsure of how they sit together.

### What AlphaFold 2 does not do

- It predicts **one chain alone**, in **one state**: no DNA, no ligand, no partner
  protein, no movement. (AlphaFold 3, 2024, adds complexes with DNA, RNA and small
  molecules: try the free [AlphaFold Server](https://alphafoldserver.com).)
- It needs **relatives**: a protein with few known relatives has a poor alignment, and a
  poor prediction.
- It is not reliable to predict the **effect of a single mutation**: the prediction of the
  mutant usually looks like the normal protein.
- A prediction is a **hypothesis**, to be checked with experiments, like a GWAS peak.

### See it for yourself

Drag the molecule to turn it, scroll to zoom, hover an amino acid to read its name,
position and pLDDT. Try:

1. ***FLC*, colour "AlphaFold confidence", style "Cartoon"**: the dark blue part is the
   MADS-box, which grips DNA; the orange tail floats around (switch the colour to
   "Domains" to check).
2. **RuBisCO, colour "Chemistry", style "Surface"**, then "Cartoon": a protein that lives
   in water hides most of its hydrophobic (yellow) amino acids inside, where water cannot
   reach them; this is what drives folding. In this model, 46% of the buried amino acids
   are hydrophobic, but only 31% of those at the surface. The yellow patches left outside
   are a clue: in the chloroplast, 8 large and 8 small RuBisCO chains assemble into one
   enzyme, and chains often stick to each other by such patches.
3. **HKT1, the same**: much more yellow on its surface (41% of its surface amino acids are
   hydrophobic). It does not live in water but inside the membrane of root cells,
   surrounded by fatty lipids. Turn it: where would the membrane be?
4. **Any protein, colour "Start to end"**: follow the chain from blue to red; the two ends
   of a chain are often far apart in space.

## Vocabulary

| Term | In one sentence |
|---|---|
| Label | The answer the model must learn to predict (the species). |
| Feature | What the model looks at to predict (a measure, a pixel). |
| Training / validation / test set | Data to learn from / to tune and decide when to stop / to judge at the end, never seen before. |
| Parameter, weight | A number learned during training (a threshold of a tree, a weight of a network). |
| Hyperparameter | A setting chosen before training (depth of a tree, number of neurons, epochs). |
| Loss | The error of the model on the training data, which training makes smaller. |
| Epoch | One pass of training over all the training examples. |
| Gradient descent | The step-by-step method that moves each weight a little to reduce the loss. |
| Overfitting | Learning the training examples by heart: good on them, poor on new data. |
| Underfitting | A model too simple to capture the rule. |
| Generalisation | Doing well on new data: the real goal. |
| Confusion matrix | Truth in rows, predictions in columns: where the model is right and how it is wrong. |
| Accuracy | Share of correct predictions, all classes together. |
| Recall | Of the true members of a class, the share found. |
| Precision | Of the predictions of a class, the share that is right. |
| Class imbalance | Some classes have many more examples than others. |
| Decision tree | A sequence of yes/no questions on the features, learned from examples. |
| Random forest | Many trees on random samples, which vote. |
| Bootstrap | Drawing the examples again at random, with replacement. |
| Neuron | A weighted sum plus a constant (a linear model), passed through an activation. |
| Activation (ReLU, sigmoid) | The function that bends the output of a neuron. |
| Layer, hidden layer | Neurons side by side; hidden = between the input and the output. |
| Convolution, filter | A small grid of weights that slides over an image and detects a pattern. |
| Pooling | Shrinking an image by keeping the largest value of each small square. |
| CNN | A network of convolution layers, for images. |
| Transfer learning, fine-tuning | Starting from a network trained on other images and retraining it on yours. |
| Annotation, consensus, ground truth | The labels made by people, the majority answer, and what we take as true. |
| Inference | Using a trained model on new data. |
| Domain shift | New data unlike the training data (other cameras, places, microscopes). |
| Hallucination | A confident but invented answer of a generative model. |
| Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) | Related sequences aligned position by position (Session 3). |
| Coevolution | Two positions of a protein that change together during evolution, often because they touch. |
| pLDDT | AlphaFold's confidence for each amino acid (0-100). |
| PAE | AlphaFold's expected error of position between two amino acids (Å). |
| Disordered region | A part of a protein without a fixed 3D shape. |
| Attention | A layer where each position weighs all the others to decide which ones matter. |
| Template | A related protein whose structure was solved by experiment. |
| Hydrophobic core | The water-fearing amino acids packed inside a soluble protein. |

## Your R toolbox

New tools today, on top of those of Sessions 4-6. `rpart` and `nnet` are installed with R:
nothing to install.

::: panel-tabset
## Train and test

Keep the test data aside **before** training:

```r
train <- my_data %>% filter(split == "train")
test  <- my_data %>% filter(split == "test")
```

## A decision tree

```r
library(rpart)
tree <- rpart(label ~ feature_1 + feature_2, data = train)
tree                          # the questions, as text
plot(tree, margin = 0.1)      # the tree as a figure
text(tree, use.n = TRUE)

predicted <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")
```

`rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 2)` lets a tree grow without limit.

## Confusion matrix

```r
table(truth = test$label, predicted = predicted)   # rows = truth, columns = prediction
mean(predicted == test$label)                       # accuracy
```

Recall of a class: its diagonal cell divided by the total of its **row**. Precision: the
diagonal cell divided by the total of its **column**.

## A loop

A `for` loop repeats the same lines for each value of `i`:

```r
for (i in 1:3) {
  print(i * 10)
}
```

`slice_sample(data, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)` draws a bootstrap sample;
`sample(x, 2)` draws 2 values of `x` at random.

## A neural network

```r
library(nnet)
net <- nnet(factor(label) ~ feature_1 + feature_2, data = train, size = 2, maxit = 500)
length(net$wts)                              # number of weights learned
predict(net, test, type = "class")
```

`size` is the number of neurons in the hidden layer. Scale the features first (mean 0,
standard deviation 1).

## A structure file

A PDB file is a text file with fixed columns: one `ATOM` line per atom.

```r
lines <- read_lines("data/my_protein.pdb")
ca <- lines[str_starts(lines, "ATOM") & substr(lines, 13, 16) == " CA "]   # alpha carbons
as.numeric(substr(ca, 31, 38))     # x (Å); y is 39-46, z 47-54
as.numeric(substr(ca, 61, 66))     # in AlphaFold files: the pLDDT
as.matrix(dist(coordinates))       # distances between all pairs of points
```

To download from R, the AlphaFold server wants a browser name:
`options(HTTPUserAgent = "Mozilla/5.0")` first.

## A matrix as an image

```r
m <- matrix(values, nrow = n_rows, byrow = TRUE)   # fill row by row
dim(m)
t(m)                                                # turn by a quarter (transpose)
m[2:4, 5:7]                                         # rows 2 to 4, columns 5 to 7
pmax(m, 0)                                          # negative values set to 0 (ReLU)
```
:::

### B. Rules by hand, then rules learned (pairs)

*Theory: [Theory 1](#theory-1) (vocabulary, confusion matrix) and the decision tree of
[Theory 2](#theory-2).*

The [Palmer penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/) (Gorman et al., 2014):
three species measured at Palmer Station, Antarctica.

- **B1**: plot two measures, and find by eye what separates the species.
- **B2**: write your own rules with `case_when()`, and measure their accuracy: this is
  programming *before* machine learning.
- **B3**: put the test penguins aside, and let `rpart()` learn the rules from the training
  penguins. Compare its questions with yours.
- **B4**: predict the test penguins, read the confusion matrix, and compute a recall and a
  precision by hand.

::: callout-note
## Checkpoint

The tree has three leaves, one per species, and its questions use two of the four
measures. The confusion matrix of B4 is a 3 × 3 table whose numbers add up to the number of
test penguins.
:::

### C. Learning or memorising? (pairs)

*Theory: [Theory 2](#theory-2) (overfitting, random forest).*

- **C1**: a tree without limit, compared with the small one, on the training and the test
  penguins.
- **C2**: shuffle the species of the training penguins, and train the same tree: what can
  it learn?
- **C3**: a random forest built by hand with a `for` loop: 100 trees, each on a bootstrap
  sample and two random measures, which vote.

::: callout-note
## Checkpoint

C1 prints a small table with two rows (small tree, deep tree) and their numbers of leaves,
training and test accuracies. C3 prints the votes of 8 trees for 5 penguins (species
names), one accuracy for the forest, and a summary of the accuracies of the 100 trees.
:::

### D. A small neural network (pairs)

*Theory: [Theory 2](#theory-2) (a neuron is a linear model).*

- **D1**: scale the measures, train a network with 2 hidden neurons, watch the loss fall in
  the Console, count its weights by hand.
- **D2**: networks of 1, 2, 10 and 100 hidden neurons: more weights, better predictions?

::: callout-note
## Checkpoint

During D1, the Console prints `initial value`, a few `iter ... value` lines, then
`converged`. D2 prints a table of four rows: hidden neurons, weights, training and test
accuracy.
:::

### E. A photo is a table of numbers (pairs)

*Theory: [Theory 3](#theory-3) (a photo is numbers, convolution).*

A photo from the [Caltech Camera Traps](https://lila.science/datasets/caltech-camera-traps)
dataset (California, CDLA-Permissive licence), in grey levels.

- **E1**: draw the photo from its table of pixels.
- **E2**: three 3 × 3 filters (vertical edges, horizontal edges, blur), applied with a
  convolution written in R.
- **E3**: filter, ReLU, pooling: one layer of a CNN, computed by hand.

::: callout-note
## Checkpoint

E1 draws the photo in black and white: a culvert, the ground, and an animal. E2 draws three
images of almost the same size, each bringing out different structures. In E3, `dim()`
shows that the image is about half as high and half as wide after the layer.
:::

### F. Deep learning for real (pairs)

*Theory: [Theory 3](#theory-3) (where the labels come from) and the confusion matrix of
[Theory 1](#theory-1).*

A ResNet-18 trained in AnnoTrain to recognise the animals photographed by camera traps along
a railway line: mostly amphibians, 10 classes.

- **F1**: its training curves: the loss on the training and validation photos, epoch after
  epoch.
- **F2**: its confusion matrix, its accuracy and the recall of each species.
- **F3**: three versions of another AnnoTrain model (vegetables), trained on more and more
  annotated photos.
- **F4**: your own annotations of the beginning of the session.

::: callout-note
## Checkpoint

F1 draws two curves over 40 epochs. F2 prints one accuracy, a table of 10 classes sorted by
their number of photos, and a heatmap with the annotated classes in rows and the predicted
ones in columns.
:::

### G. AlphaFold: from a sequence to a structure (then after class)

*Theory: [Theory 4](#theory-4), and its 3D viewer.*

*FLC* (Session 6) has never been solved by experiment: AlphaFold predicted it.

- **G1**, in the **Terminal**: ask the AlphaFold database about *FLC*, download its
  structure, and look inside with the commands of Session 1:

```bash
cd ~/bioinfo_course/session_07/data
curl -s https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/api/prediction/Q9S7Q7 | head -c 700
curl -s -A "Mozilla/5.0" -o FLC_live.pdb https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/files/AF-Q9S7Q7-F1-model_v6.pdb
head -n 4 FLC_live.pdb
grep "^ATOM" FLC_live.pdb | head -n 3
grep "^ATOM" FLC_live.pdb | wc -l
grep "^ATOM" FLC_live.pdb | grep " CA " | wc -l
```

  (`-A "Mozilla/5.0"` gives a browser name: without it, the server answers `403
  Forbidden`. If the network fails, the same file is already in `data/`.)

- **G2**: read the structure as a table in R, and plot the confidence (pLDDT) along the
  sequence, with the two domains of *FLC* described in UniProt.
- **G3**: draw the structure from its coordinates, then look at it in 3D: in the viewer of
  Theory 4 ("See it for yourself"), and by opening **your own downloaded file** in
  [Mol\* Viewer](https://molstar.org/viewer/) (the viewer of the Protein Data Bank and of
  AlphaFold DB).
- **G4**: the contact map: which amino acids touch in 3D.
- **G5**: the PAE: how sure AlphaFold is of the position of each domain relative to the
  other.
- **G6**: how coevolution reveals contacts, on a small made-up alignment.
- **G7**, alone: *FLC*, the RuBisCO of photosynthesis and *HKT1*, the sodium transporter of
  Session 6: which one is predicted best, and why?

::: callout-note
## Checkpoint

In G1, the first command prints text starting with `[{"toolUsed":`, and the last one prints
the number of amino acids of *FLC*. G2 draws one line between 0 and 100 over two shaded
domains, and counts the amino acids in four bands. G4 and G5 draw two square maps of the
same size, with a dark diagonal. G6 finds one pair of positions. G7 prints a table of
three proteins.
:::

### H. A tour of AI in biology (after class, on your own)

Open at least four of these tools (AlphaFold does not count: you explored it in block G),
use each one for real, and fill the table of H1. At least one that identifies a living
being.

| Tool | What it does | Type of AI |
|---|---|---|
| [Pl@ntNet](https://identify.plantnet.org) | Identifies a plant from a photo (leaf, flower, bark). | Classification (CNN), labels from botanists and citizens |
| [iNaturalist](https://www.inaturalist.org) | Suggests the species of any observation; the community confirms ("research grade"). | Classification + human consensus |
| [Merlin Bird ID](https://merlin.allaboutbirds.org) / [BirdNET](https://birdnet.cornell.edu) | Identifies birds from their song: the sound becomes a spectrogram, an image read by a CNN. | Classification of sounds |
| [AlphaFold Protein Structure Database](https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk) / [AlphaFold Server](https://alphafoldserver.com) | Block G. Also try the spike of SARS-CoV-2 ([P0DTC2](https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P0DTC2)) from Session 3, or predict a complex on the Server. | Structure prediction (deep learning) |
| [ESM Metagenomic Atlas](https://esmatlas.com) | 600 million predicted structures of proteins from environmental DNA, by a protein language model. | Self-supervised language model |
| [Cellpose](https://www.cellpose.org) | Upload a microscopy image: each cell is outlined. | Segmentation (U-Net style) |
| [Teachable Machine](https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com) | Train your own image classifier in the browser with your webcam (two classes: a leaf and a pen, for example), then try to fool it. | Transfer learning |
| [TensorFlow Playground](https://playground.tensorflow.org) | A neural network you can watch learn: add neurons and layers, add noise, see overfitting. | Neural network |
| [CNN Explainer](https://poloclub.github.io/cnn-explainer/) | Every convolution of a small CNN, interactive. | CNN |
| [AnnoTrain](https://annotrain.cmaslard.xyz) | Annotate, see the consensus, the models and their mistakes. | Annotation + classification, detection, segmentation |
| [Wildlife Insights](https://www.wildlifeinsights.org) / [MegaDetector](https://github.com/agentmorris/MegaDetector) | Camera-trap photos sorted automatically: empty or animal, then species. | Detection + classification |
| [DeepLabCut](https://www.deeplabcut.org) | Follows the body parts of an animal in a video (behaviour). | Pose estimation |
| A chatbot (ChatGPT, Claude, Le Chat, Copilot...) | Answers questions, explains and writes code. | Generative AI (large language model) |

### Using AI well as a biologist

- **Use an existing tool first.** Many questions already have a trained model (Pl@ntNet,
  BirdNET, MegaDetector, Cellpose, AlphaFold). Train your own (AnnoTrain, Teachable Machine)
  only when none fits.
- **Check it on your own data.** A model trained elsewhere can fail on your cameras, your
  region, your microscope (domain shift). Annotate a sample yourself and compute the recall
  per class before trusting the counts.
- **Look at more than the accuracy**: the confusion matrix, the recall of the rare classes,
  the photos where the model is unsure.
- **Report what you used**: the tool, its version, its settings, and how you checked it.
- **Chatbots are excellent assistants and unreliable sources.** Ask them to explain an
  error message or a line of code, to suggest a plot; never trust a number, a reference
  or a fact without checking it (block G2). They write fluent text even when they invent.
- **Do not paste** unpublished data, personal data, or confidential documents into an
  online AI: you remain responsible for them.

## Checkpoint

You are done when all of the following are true:

- you can explain, with the chihuahua and the muffin, why machine learning exists;
- you can place AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI in each other;
- you trained a decision tree and read its questions;
- you can read a confusion matrix and compute an accuracy, a recall and a precision;
- you can explain overfitting, and why a model is judged on a test set;
- you can explain why a forest of trees votes better than one tree;
- you can say what a neuron, a weight, a loss and an epoch are;
- you computed a convolution, and can say what the filters of a CNN learn;
- you can explain why an accuracy of 87% can hide a poor model for rare species;
- you can explain how an alignment and coevolution let AlphaFold predict a
  structure, and judge a prediction with its pLDDT and PAE;
- you used four AI tools for biology, and checked the answer of a chatbot.

## Optional challenge

For your own interest.

**A. A real random forest.** Install the package `randomForest` (`install.packages("randomForest")`,
about a minute) and run `randomForest(factor(species) ~ bill_len + bill_dep + flipper_len + body_mass, data = train)`.
Compare its accuracy with your hand-made forest, and look at `importance()`.

**B. A training curve of your own.** Train the network of D1 with `maxit = 1, 2, 5, 10, 20,
50` (same `set.seed(3)` before each) and plot the training and test accuracy against the
number of iterations.

**C. Fool Teachable Machine.** Train it on two objects in front of a plain wall, then show
them in front of a busy background. What did it really learn?

**E. Your own protein.** Pick any protein you care about on [UniProt](https://www.uniprot.org),
then in R: `options(HTTPUserAgent = "Mozilla/5.0")`,
`info <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/api/prediction/ACCESSION")`, and
`download.file(info$pdbUrl, "data/my_protein.pdb")`. Redo G2-G4 on it.

**D. A live model.** The AnnoTrain models are public: in R,
`jsonlite::fromJSON("https://annotrain.cmaslard.xyz/api/projects/caltech-test/models")`
returns every version of the camera-trap model with its metrics. Find the history of the
latest version and plot its curves.
